subject: Chemistry
title: Introduction to Chemistry — Meaning and Branches
content:
Chemistry is the study of the composition, structure, properties and changes of matter.

Branches: Organic chemistry (carbon compounds), Inorganic chemistry (non-carbon), Physical chemistry (energy & rates), Analytical chemistry (identifying substances), Biochemistry (chemistry of life).

Careers: pharmacy, medicine, petroleum engineering, food science, brewing.
keyPoints: Chemistry studies matter and its changes
Organic = carbon compounds; Inorganic = the rest
Analytical chemistry identifies and quantifies substances

subject: Chemistry
title: Laboratory Apparatus and Their Uses
content:
Common apparatus:
• Beaker — holding/mixing liquids (not for accurate measuring)
• Measuring cylinder — measuring volumes of liquid
• Burette — accurate delivery of liquid in titration (0.1 cm³)
• Pipette — fixed accurate volume (e.g. 25 cm³)
• Conical (titration) flask, round-bottom flask
• Bunsen burner — heating; tripod stand, wire gauze, clamp
• Funnel, filter paper — separation
• Test tube & holder, evaporating dish, desiccator
keyPoints: Burette/pipette for accurate volumes; beaker is approximate
Bunsen burner: luminous (yellow, sooty, cooler) vs non-luminous (blue, hotter) flame
Never heat apparatus that is cracked

subject: Chemistry
title: Safety Rules in the Laboratory
content:
1. Follow instructions; never taste or smell chemicals directly.
2. Wear safety goggles and lab coat; tie back long hair.
3. Keep flammables away from flames; point test tubes away from people when heating.
4. Report all accidents/spills immediately.
5. Know where the fire extinguisher, first-aid box and exits are.
6. Wash hands after experiments; never pipette by mouth.
7. Dispose of waste as directed — never pour chemicals down the sink unless told.
keyPoints: Never taste chemicals; waft to smell
Point heated test tubes away from people
Know emergency equipment locations

subject: Chemistry
title: Matter — States and Properties
content:
Matter is anything with mass that occupies space. Three states:
• Solid — fixed shape/volume, particles tightly packed, vibrate in place
• Liquid — fixed volume, takes container's shape, particles close but mobile
• Gas — no fixed shape/volume, particles far apart, move fast and randomly

Changes of state: melting (solid→liquid), freezing, evaporation/boiling (liquid→gas), condensation, sublimation (solid→gas directly, e.g. iodine, camphor, dry ice).
keyPoints: Solid/liquid/gas differences = particle arrangement & energy
Melting point of ice = 0°C; boiling point of water = 100°C
Sublimation: solid straight to gas

subject: Chemistry
title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
content:
Element — one kind of atom only (O₂, Fe, Cu). 118 known elements, arranged in the Periodic Table.
Compound — two or more elements chemically joined in fixed ratio (H₂O, CO₂, NaCl). Properties differ from constituent elements; can only be split by chemical means.
Mixture — substances physically combined in any ratio (air, salt water, soil). Separated by physical means.

Symbols to know: H, C, N, O, Na (sodium), K (potassium), Ca, Fe, Cu, Zn, Al, Pb, Ag, Hg.
keyPoints: Element: one atom type; Compound: chemical bond, fixed ratio; Mixture: physical, any ratio
Compounds need chemical reactions to separate; mixtures need physical methods
Know first 20 element symbols

subject: Chemistry
title: Separation Techniques
content:
Choose the technique based on the mixture's properties:
• Filtration — insoluble solid from liquid (sand + water)
• Evaporation — dissolved solid from liquid (salt from brine)
• Distillation — two liquids with different boiling points (or get pure solvent); fractional distillation separates close boiling points (petroleum refining!)
• Separating funnel — immiscible liquids (oil + water)
• Magnet — magnetic from non-magnetic (iron filings + sulphur)
• Sublimation — sublimable solid (iodine from salt)
• Chromatography — coloured dyes/pigments
• Decantation, centrifugation, crystallisation.
keyPoints: Filtration vs evaporation: insoluble vs dissolved solid
Fractional distillation = crude oil refining
Chromatography separates dyes by adsorption

subject: Chemistry
title: Physical and Chemical Changes
content:
Physical change — no new substance formed, usually reversible: melting ice, dissolving sugar, magnetising iron, breaking glass.
Chemical change — new substance formed with different properties, usually irreversible, involves energy change: rusting, burning, souring milk, photosynthesis.

Test signs of chemical change: colour change, gas given off, precipitate formed, heat/light given out or absorbed, new smell.
keyPoints: Physical: reversible, no new substance
Chemical: new substance + energy change
Rusting = iron + oxygen + water (chemical)

subject: Chemistry
title: Atomic Theory
content:
Dalton (1808): matter made of indivisible atoms; atoms of same element identical.
J.J. Thomson: discovered the electron — 'plum pudding' model.
Rutherford (1911): gold-foil experiment — atom is mostly empty space with a tiny dense positive nucleus.
Bohr: electrons orbit in fixed shells/energy levels.

Sub-atomic particles: proton (positive, in nucleus), neutron (neutral, nucleus), electron (negative, shells). Atomic number Z = protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons.
keyPoints: Electron: Thomson; nucleus: Rutherford; shells: Bohr
Proton +1, neutron 0, electron −1
Z = protons, A = p + n; isotopes = same Z, different A

subject: Chemistry
title: Structure of the Atom — Electron Configuration
content:
Electrons fill shells in order: 1st shell max 2, 2nd max 8, 3rd max 8 (SS1 level).
Examples: Na (11) = 2,8,1; Cl (17) = 2,8,7; O (8) = 2,6.

Valence electrons (outermost shell) decide chemistry: Na has 1 → loses it to become Na⁺; Cl has 7 → gains one to become Cl⁻. Opposite charges attract = ionic bond.

Isotopes: atoms of same element with same protons but different neutrons, e.g. Cl-35 and Cl-37.
keyPoints: Shell capacities: 2, 8, 8
Group number ≈ valence electrons; period = shells
Isotopes: same Z, different A
